summary:
Bulgaria does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression. Same-sex relations have been decriminalised since 1968, no statute regulates which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender, and border and visa rules are applied to foreign passports on ordinary terms. A visitor's recorded gender raises no separate question on entry.

Domestic legal recognition of a trans person's gender is refused in law and in judicial policy. The Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 holds that the only meaning of the term sex is its biological one and that the legal system rests on the binary existence of humankind, effectively barring legal gender change; the Constitutional Court's Istanbul Convention verdict condemned the legislation that would permit it. The European Court of Human Rights found an Article 8 violation in Y.T. v Bulgaria in 2020 over refusal of recognition, held in December 2024 that those obligations were unaffected by the registry revision of that year, and Judge Šimáčková dissented that the revision decision was over-formalistic. In September 2025 an Advocate General of the Court of Justice of the European Union, Richard de la Tour, opined that EU law precludes legislation such as Bulgaria's refusing identity documents matching a trans person's presented gender, and the court concurred with that reasoning; the full judgment was still pending.

The statutory baseline for a visitor refused a service is partial. The Protection Against Discrimination Act, in force since 1 January 2004, prohibits direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment and bans hate speech based on sexual orientation, and a 2015 amendment extended coverage to sex as including sex change. Gender expression and gender identity are not explicitly named in that 2015 revision, so a claimant must argue within a category written around sex and sexual orientation.

Enforcement against bias violence is the weakest point of the framework. Amnesty International's 2015 review found that legislation exists but that authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes, with the Sofia Prosecution opening only some cases. Attacks inherited that pattern: the 2008 killing of a 25-year-old student in a Sofia park by a group intending to cleanse the park of gays, and the assault in Plovdiv on 27 September 2020 on children as young as 14 or 15 by ultra-fans of Botev, described as an anti-LGBT cleansing action. A January 2014 government commitment to outlaw such hate crimes was dropped by the government formed after the October 2014 elections, though heavier penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation were adopted on 28 July 2023.

Public visibility carries a documented risk of organised hostility, and order at Pride events has historically depended on heavy police presence. The first Sofia Pride in 2008, with about 150 participants, was attacked with petrol bombs, rocks and glass bottles and over 60 hooligans were arrested; far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions; the fourth annual march in June 2011 passed without incident under heavy police guard while a group styling itself a family NGO protested. In June 2017 Human Rights Watch urged authorities to protect the march after a group called the National Resistance rallied counter-demonstrators to cleanse Sofia from garbage, a movement that advocated brooms and shovels against attendees.

Recognition of a visitor's relationship is refused. Article 46 of the Constitution has defined marriage as a union between a man and a woman since 1991, no civil unions exist, and same-sex couples are consequently denied inheritance, joint property and medical decision-making rights; same-sex couples are also banned from adopting. A Sofia court granted residency in June 2018 to an Australian woman and her French wife married in France in 2016, applying the Coman ruling, after their earlier denial, while the Sofia Administrative Court rejected a recognition claim in January 2018 for a couple married in the United Kingdom, an appeal pursued by the LGBT organisation Deystvie. The European Court of Human Rights held in September 2023 that Bulgaria's refusal to recognise same-sex couples is an infringement of human rights, a case subject to appeal. A court recognised a same-sex marriage performed in France in 2019, and a 2021 Court of Justice ruling forced Bulgaria to issue an ID to a child of a lesbian couple after it refused a birth certificate.
tangentialFactors:
The direction of official policy is downward rather than stable. On 7 August 2024 the National Assembly passed an amendment to the education law prohibiting propaganda, promotion or incitement, directly or indirectly, of ideas about non-traditional sexual orientation and non-biological gender identity in the education system; it was signed by President Rumen Radev and took effect on 16 August 2024, introduced by the Revival party and backed by GERB. The same impulse produced a November 2009 District Council of Pazardzhik vote forbidding public demonstration of sexual or any other orientation, which the Administrative Court struck down in October 2010 on procedural grounds and then upheld on appeal in July 2011.

Institutional hostility is reinforced by public speech. The Bulgarian Orthodox Church describes Pride events as a sinful demonstration, billboards promoting tolerance toward same-sex couples in Varna and Burgas were vandalised in December 2018, and the Ataka party has protested Pride. Anti-LGBT rhetoric rose sharply in 2020 and 2021, during which gender became a slur in public discourse. The 1964 show trial of 26 men, including actor Georgi Partsalev and singer Emil Dimitrov, was described by experts as a masquerade for the public about decadent Western culture and remains the reference point for how same-sex conduct was once prosecuted.

ILGA-Europe ranked Bulgaria 37th of 49 European countries for LGBT rights protection in 2020, a position consistent with the layered protections and simultaneous recognition ban described above. The age of consent has been 14 regardless of sex since 2002 and is 16 as of 2026.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change is blocked for residents by the Supreme Court of Cassation's interpretative decision of 20 February 2023 and by the Constitutional Court's Istanbul Convention verdict, and the registry revision of 2024 was held in December 2024 not to satisfy the European Court of Human Rights' 2020 Article 8 finding in Y.T. v Bulgaria.

The 2024 education law amendment constrains what schools may say about gender identity other than the biological one, and it operates alongside the Pazardzhik council prohibition on public demonstration of orientation that survived on appeal in July 2011. Hate speech based on sexual orientation has been banned since the Protection Against Discrimination Act took effect on 1 January 2004, but gender expression and gender identity are not explicitly named in the 2015 revision of that Act.

Intersex newborns routinely have male genitalia removed as the easier operation, with parents rarely informed of later harm to the child's gender identity, and there are no laws concerning intersex people. Health services are covered by the anti-discrimination ban on sexual-orientation discrimination in force since 1 January 2004, but same-sex couples are denied the right to make medical decisions for each other. Gay and bisexual men are not explicitly barred from donating blood: the donor form, under a Ministry of Healthcare ordinance of 19 July 2004, does not ask orientation but requires confirmation of no HIV or STI-risk practices.

Support infrastructure exists at limited scale. Single Step Foundation, founded in 2016, works with LGBTI youth on coming out and affirmation, and in October 2017 it launched Bulgaria's first licensed online support chat for LGBTI youth, families and allies.

Same-sex couples are denied marriage under Article 46 of the Constitution and have no civil union to fall back on, which removes inheritance, joint property, medical decision-making and adoption rights. A 2008 survey of 15 schools in Sofia, Varna and Plovdiv found 10.5 per cent of students identifying as bisexual and 1.8 per cent as gay, with 29 per cent saying they would refuse to sit next to a gay classmate and 39 per cent saying they would protect one.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the gender marker on a visitor's foreign passport is accepted without comment by Bulgarian authorities in practice, beyond the ordinary application of entry rules, is not addressed by the sources and remains unresolved here.

The Court of Justice of the European Union opinion reported in September 2025 is an Advocate General's opinion with the court's concurrence on the reasoning; the full judgment and its timing are not stated in the inventory and are unresolved.

The September 2023 European Court of Human Rights finding on non-recognition of same-sex couples is recorded as subject to appeal and awaiting a government response, so its operative effect is unresolved.

The Pazardzhik council prohibition is reported both as struck down in October 2010 for procedural errors and as upheld on appeal in July 2011; the inventory does not reconcile which version governs today.

The Amnesty International account of investigative failure dates from February 2015 and the 2014 government commitment it discusses was dropped that year; whether the heavier penalties adopted on 28 July 2023 have changed prosecutorial practice is not sourced.
